title: Longest Palindromic Subsequence
directAnswer: Find the longest subsequence of s that reads the same forwards and backwards. Two equivalent framings: (1) interval DP where dp[i][j] is the LPS length of s[i..j] — if the ends match, dp[i][j] = 2 + dp[i+1][j-1], else max(dp[i+1][j], dp[i][j-1]); base dp[i][i] = 1; (2) the LCS of s and reverse(s). Both are O(n²) time. The interval view is the cleaner derivation; the reverse-LCS view is the slickest one-liner reduction.

remember.pattern: Interval DP on [i, j] — match the two ends or drop one of them
remember.formula:
dp[i][i] = 1
if s[i] == s[j]: dp[i][j] = 2 + dp[i+1][j-1]
else:            dp[i][j] = max(dp[i+1][j], dp[i][j-1])
answer = dp[0][n-1]
# alt: LPS(s) == LCS(s, reverse(s))
rules: Subsequence, **not** substring — you may delete characters but not reorder them, so the picks needn't be contiguous.
When the two ends match, they **both** join the palindrome: `dp[i][j] = 2 + dp[i+1][j-1]`.
When the ends differ, **drop one end** and take the better side: `max(dp[i+1][j], dp[i][j-1])`.
Base case is a single character (`dp[i][i] = 1`); an empty interval contributes 0.
Fill by **increasing interval length** (or iterate `i` downward, `j` upward) so the inner interval `[i+1, j-1]` is ready first.
whenToUse: Longest palindromic structure where you may skip characters (subsequence, not substring)
Minimum insertions/deletions to make a string a palindrome (n − LPS)
Any 'match the two ends or shrink from one side' interval problem on a single string
Reductions to LCS where the second string is the reverse of the first
antiSignals: You need a CONTIGUOUS palindrome → Longest Palindromic Substring (expand-around-center or different DP)
You need the actual subsequence string → reconstruct from the table, still O(n²)
Counting distinct palindromic subsequences → a different, harder DP with inclusion-exclusion
n is huge (millions) → O(n²) too slow; the problem usually caps n at a few thousand
remember.takeaway: Longest Palindromic Subsequence is the 'match the ends' interval DP. If the boundary characters agree they both join the palindrome and you recurse inward; if not, you discard one boundary and keep the better side. Equivalently it's LCS(s, reverse(s)). The same dp drives minimum insertions to form a palindrome — that answer is just n minus the LPS.

interviewerIntent.testing: Whether you recognise an interval DP on [i, j], handle the two cases (ends equal → +2 and shrink both; ends differ → drop one end), and can connect it to LCS of s and its reverse.
interviewerIntent.commonMistake: Solving Longest Palindromic SUBSTRING by mistake, using max() when the ends match instead of adding 2, or filling the table in an order where [i+1][j-1] isn't ready yet.
interviewerIntent.toStandOut: Offer both derivations — the direct interval DP and the LCS(s, reverse(s)) reduction — and note that minimum insertions to make s a palindrome equals n − LPS, showing you see the family of problems.

problemStatement:
Given a string `s`, find the length of the ***longest palindromic subsequence*** in `s`.

A **subsequence** is a sequence derived from `s` by deleting zero or more characters without changing the order of the remaining characters. A **palindrome** reads the same forwards and backwards.

Return the length of the longest such subsequence (you do not need to return the subsequence itself).
constraints: s consists only of lowercase English letters
The answer is at least 1 (any single character is a palindrome of length 1)
understanding: Picture choosing characters from s, keeping their order, so the chosen sequence is a palindrome — and make it as long as possible. Working from the two ends inward: if the first and last characters of the current window are equal, they can both sit at the outside of a palindrome, contributing 2 and leaving the inner window to solve. If they differ, at least one of them can't be a matched outer pair, so you discard one end and take whichever side gives more. The state is the window [i, j], which is exactly an interval DP.

clarifyingQuestions.question: Subsequence or substring?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: Subsequence — deletions are allowed, the characters needn't be contiguous. 'bbbab' has LPS 4 ('bbbb'), even though those b's aren't adjacent.

clarifyingQuestions.question: Do I return the length or the actual palindrome?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: Just the length here. Reconstructing the subsequence means walking the DP table backward from dp[0][n-1].

clarifyingQuestions.question: Is the empty string possible?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: Constraints say length ≥ 1, so the answer is at least 1. An empty interval would contribute 0 in the recurrence.

clarifyingQuestions.question: Is there a slick reduction?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: Yes — the LPS of s equals the LCS of s and reverse(s). Same O(n²) cost, sometimes easier to code if you already have an LCS routine.

examples.explanation: The subsequence 'bbbb' (indices 0,1,2,4) is a palindrome of length 4. You can't reach 5 because of the single 'a'.
'abdba' (drop the 'g') is a palindrome of length 5.

diagrams.title: Picking the right approach
diagrams.caption: The decision tree to run before writing code. 'Longest palindrome you may skip chars for' lands on the interval DP.

approaches.name: Brute Force — Recursion Matching the Two Ends
approaches.whenToMention: Say this first to establish the two-case interval recurrence (ends match vs differ), then flag the exponential overlap.
hints: Look at the two ends of the current window s[i..j]. If s[i] == s[j], can both characters be part of the same palindrome? What's left to solve?
If the ends match, they wrap a palindrome: count 2 and recurse on the inner window [i+1, j-1]. If they differ, at least one end is useless — drop one side.
When the ends differ, try both: solve(i+1, j) and solve(i, j-1), and take the max. Base cases: i > j → 0, i == j → 1.
approaches.complexityReasoning: When the ends differ the recursion forks into two overlapping subproblems; the unmemoized tree is exponential. Recursion depth is O(n).
approaches.explanation:
Define `solve(i, j)` = length of the longest palindromic subsequence of the window `s[i..j]`.

- If `i > j` the window is empty → 0.
- If `i == j` it's a single character, itself a palindrome → 1.
- If `s[i] == s[j]`, both ends can serve as the outer pair of a palindrome, contributing 2, and the rest comes from the inner window: `2 + solve(i+1, j-1)`.
- Otherwise the ends differ; at least one of them cannot be an outer matched character, so drop one and take the better side: `max(solve(i+1, j), solve(i, j-1))`.

**The mental shift: decide the fate of the two boundary characters.** A palindrome is defined by its symmetry around the center, so the natural question at any window is what happens at its outermost characters. If they're equal, the greedy-looking move — pair them up and recurse inward — is provably optimal: any palindromic subsequence of `[i, j]` can be extended to use both equal ends without getting shorter. If they're unequal, they can't both be the matched outer pair, so the optimum must ignore at least one of them, which is exactly the two `max` branches.

**Why `+2`, not `+1` or `max`, when the ends match.** Both `s[i]` and `s[j]` join the palindrome — one on the left flank, one on the right — so they add two characters, and the inner window is solved independently. Using `max` here (a classic slip) throws away the guaranteed pair and undercounts.

**Why we don't ship this.** The two `max` branches overlap enormously — `solve(i+1, j)` and `solve(i, j-1)` both recurse into `solve(i+1, j-1)`, and so on — so the same window is recomputed exponentially many times. Caching `solve(i, j)` collapses it to `O(n²)`.
approaches.insight: The state is the window `(i, j)` — a contiguous interval — and the recursion repeatedly revisits the same window through different end-dropping choices. Interval state plus heavy overlap is the textbook signal for an O(n²) interval DP.

dryRun.intro: solve(i, j) on windows. Match ends → 2 + inner; differ → max of dropping one end.

java.explanation: A single character is a palindrome of length 1 — the diagonal base case.
Matching ends both join the palindrome — add 2 and shrink the window on both sides.

java.line: return Math.max(solve(s, i + 1, j), solve(s, i, j - 1));
java.explanation: Differing ends: drop the left or the right end, keep the better side.

python.line:
if s[i] == s[j]:
            return 2 + solve(i + 1, j - 1)
python.explanation: Both ends pair up; the inner window is solved independently.
These two branches overlap heavily — the reason caching is needed.

edgeCases.behavior: Every end pair matches, recursing straight inward → returns n.

pitfalls: Using max() when the ends match instead of adding 2 — silently undercounts.
Forgetting the i > j empty-window base case — infinite recursion or wrong counts on even-length matches.
Skipping this approach — verbalising the end-matching recurrence is what the interviewer wants.

approaches.name: Top-Down Memoization on (i, j)
approaches.whenToMention: The fix once you name the overlap — 'cache solve(i, j) so each window is computed once'.
hints: solve(i, j) returns the same value every call. Where can you store it so each window is computed once?
Use a 2-D memo of size n × n indexed by the window endpoints. Check on entry, fill before returning; use -1 for 'uncomputed' (real lengths are ≥ 0).
There are O(n²) windows and each does O(1) work → O(n²) time and space.
approaches.complexityReasoning: There are O(n²) distinct (i, j) windows; each combines its sub-results in O(1) → O(n²) time. The memo is O(n²); recursion depth is O(n) on top.
approaches.explanation:
Keep the end-matching recurrence but cache `solve(i, j)` in a 2-D table so each window is solved once.

**The mental shift: a window's LPS depends only on its endpoints.** However you arrived at `[i, j]`, the longest palindromic subsequence inside it is a fixed number. Caching by `(i, j)` removes all the duplicated work. There are `O(n²)` windows and each costs `O(1)` to resolve given its sub-results, so the bound is `O(n²)` directly.

**Choosing the sentinel.** Initialise the memo to -1 for 'uncomputed' — real LPS lengths are non-negative, so -1 is unambiguous. The `i == j` base returns 1 and `i > j` returns 0 before any lookup.

**A language note (Java memo vs Python tabulation).** Recursion here nests up to `O(n)` deep. With `n` as large as 1000 (the constraint), that depth approaches **Python's default recursion limit of about 1000**, so a deep, skewed input can overflow the stack. In Java that depth is fine. So in Python you'd either raise the limit with `sys.setrecursionlimit` or prefer the bottom-up table (next approach), which has no recursion at all. Top-down memoization is the comfortable default in Java; tabulation is the safer default in Python at this size.
approaches.insight: Same mechanical upgrade: a correct recurrence plus a cache keyed on the interval `(i, j)`. The insight — pair matching ends, otherwise drop one — was found in the brute force; memoization is bookkeeping.

dryRun.intro: memo[i][j] caches the LPS of window [i, j]. Smaller windows resolve first.

java.explanation: Cache hit returns the stored window length in O(1).
Matching ends add 2 and recurse on the cached inner window.

python.explanation: n up to 1000 makes recursion depth approach Python's default limit; raise it or use tabulation.
Caches solve by (i, j) — a clean 2-D top-down memo.
Differing ends: the cached better side wins.

edgeCases.behavior: Java memo is fine; Python needs a raised limit or the bottom-up table.

pitfalls: Using 0 as the sentinel — 0 is a valid length for empty windows; use -1.
Recursing in Python at n ≈ 1000 without raising the limit — risks a stack overflow.
Caching only on one index — both endpoints define the window.

approaches.name: Bottom-Up — Interval DP by Increasing Length (Optimal)
approaches.whenToMention: The answer they want. Frame it as 'fill dp[i][j] so the inner window [i+1][j-1] is ready', and mention the LCS(s, reverse) alternative.
hints: dp[i][j] = LPS of s[i..j] needs dp[i+1][j-1], dp[i+1][j], and dp[i][j-1] — all on shorter or inner windows. Fill so those are ready first.
Set dp[i][i] = 1. Then fill by increasing window length (or iterate i from n-1 down to 0 and j from i+1 up to n-1).
If s[i]==s[j]: dp[i][j] = 2 + dp[i+1][j-1]; else max(dp[i+1][j], dp[i][j-1]). Answer dp[0][n-1].
approaches.complexityReasoning: There are O(n²) windows, each filled in O(1) → O(n²) time. The full table is O(n²); since each row depends only on the row below, two rolling rows give O(n) space.
approaches.explanation:
Build `dp[i][j]` = LPS of `s[i..j]` so that every window's dependencies are finalised before it. Seed the diagonal `dp[i][i] = 1`. Then for each window length from 2 to n, set `i`, compute `j = i + length - 1`, and apply the recurrence; the answer is `dp[0][n-1]`.

**The dependency order.** `dp[i][j]` reads `dp[i+1][j-1]` (inner window, two shorter), `dp[i+1][j]` and `dp[i][j-1]` (one shorter each). All are strictly shorter intervals, so filling by increasing length guarantees they're ready. Equivalently, iterate `i` from `n-1` down to `0` (outer) and `j` from `i+1` up to `n-1` (inner) — this also visits `[i+1][*]` before `[i][*]`. Either ordering avoids reading an unfilled cell.

**The recurrence in table terms.** If `s[i] == s[j]`, the two ends pair up: `dp[i][j] = 2 + dp[i+1][j-1]`. Otherwise drop one end: `dp[i][j] = max(dp[i+1][j], dp[i][j-1])`. The diagonal of 1s anchors everything, exactly like the single-matrix base in Matrix Chain.

**The reverse-LCS reduction.** A palindromic subsequence of `s` reads identically in `s` and in `reverse(s)`, so the longest one is precisely the Longest Common Subsequence of `s` and `reverse(s)`. If you already have an LCS routine, `LPS(s) = LCS(s, reverse(s))` is a two-line solution with the same `O(n²)` cost. Mention both framings — the interval DP shows you understand the structure; the reduction shows breadth.

**Space compression.** Because `dp[i][*]` depends only on `dp[i+1][*]` and earlier cells in the same row, keep two rows for `O(n)` space.

**Why bottom-up here.** With `n` up to 1000, the table fill has no recursion, so it sidesteps Python's stack-depth limit entirely — the practical reason to prefer it in Python.
approaches.insight: This is the 'match the two ends' interval-DP template: state = window [i, j], decision = pair the ends or shrink from one side, fill order = increasing length. The same dp answers Minimum Insertions to make a palindrome (= n − LPS). And the reverse-LCS view connects it to the whole LCS family.

Fill by increasing window length so [i+1][j-1] is already done.
Matching ends pair up: add 2 to the inner window's LPS.
Differing ends: keep the better of dropping the left or right end.

python.explanation: Increasing length guarantees shorter/inner windows are computed first.
Ends equal — both characters join the palindrome.

diagrams.title: Window dependencies in the LPS table
diagrams.caption: dp[i][j] reads the inner window [i+1][j-1] when ends match, or the one-shorter windows [i+1][j] / [i][j-1] when they differ. Fill by increasing length.

edgeCases.behavior: Every end pair matches → dp[0][n-1] = n.
The recurrence pairs every symmetric pair → returns n.

pitfalls: Iterating i, j in plain ascending order — reads dp[i+1][j-1] before it's filled.
Using max() instead of 2 + inner when the ends match — undercounts the guaranteed pair.
Confusing this with the substring version, which forbids deletions and needs a different DP.

commonMistakes: Solving Longest Palindromic SUBSTRING (contiguous) instead of subsequence.
Using max() when the two ends match rather than adding 2 and shrinking both sides.
Filling the table so the inner window dp[i+1][j-1] isn't ready when read.

commonMistakesDetailed.title: Subsequence vs substring
commonMistakesDetailed.why: Subsequence allows deletions; substring requires contiguity. On 'bbbab' the subsequence answer is 4 ('bbbb') but the longest palindromic substring is 'bbb' (length 3). Using the substring DP here undercounts.

commonMistakesDetailed.title: max() on matching ends
commonMistakesDetailed.why: When s[i]==s[j] both characters are guaranteed to extend the palindrome, so the answer is 2 + inner. Taking max(dp[i+1][j], dp[i][j-1]) ignores that pair and can return a smaller value.

commonMistakesDetailed.title: Wrong fill order
commonMistakesDetailed.why: dp[i][j] depends on dp[i+1][j-1] (inner, two shorter). Iterating i ascending and j ascending visits dp[i][j] before dp[i+1][...] exists. Fill by increasing length, or i descending with j ascending.

followupVariations.title: Longest Palindromic Substring
followupVariations.hint: Contiguous version — expand around each center or use a substring DP; deletions are not allowed.

followupVariations.title: Minimum Insertions to Make a Palindrome
followupVariations.hint: Answer is n − LPS(s) — the characters not in the longest palindromic subsequence each need a mirror inserted.

followupVariations.title: Longest Common Subsequence
followupVariations.hint: LPS(s) = LCS(s, reverse(s)) — the same O(n²) grid DP under the hood.

followupVariations.title: Count Different Palindromic Subsequences
followupVariations.hint: Count distinct palindromic subsequences — a harder interval DP with inclusion–exclusion on repeated characters.

patternNote: Canonical 'match the two ends' interval DP on a single string. Recognise it when the state is a window [i, j] and you either pair the boundary characters (when equal) or shrink from one side (when not). Fill by increasing length. Equivalently it's LCS(s, reverse(s)), and n − LPS gives the minimum insertions to form a palindrome.
